title: Data transformations: comprehensions, iteration, patterns, and JSON
sources: Python 3.14 Tutorial: data structures and looping techniques
Python 3.14 Standard Library: re and json
masterChecklist: Comprehensions and generator expressions; nesting, filters, readability trade-offs
Regular expressions: patterns, raw strings, groups, search/match/fullmatch, substitution, readability and safety
JSON, CSV, and structured-data shapes; validation and schema thinking
whyItMatters: Real programs transform collections, extract patterns from text, and exchange structured information. These tools are useful when used clearly; short code is not automatically better code.
simpleExplanation: A comprehension creates a collection from an iterable in one readable expression. A generator expression produces values lazily. Regular expressions describe text patterns; raw strings make their backslashes clearer. JSON represents simple structured data using objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null.
mentalModel: A comprehension is a small assembly line; a generator is an assembly line that makes an item only when requested; a regular expression is a carefully written stencil for text.
outcomes: Write a readable filtered list comprehension.
Explain when a generator is useful.
Use re.fullmatch for a complete simple validation pattern.
Load and validate the expected shape of simple JSON data.

realWorldExample.scenario: A course importer reads JSON records, keeps only completed lesson titles, and checks a simple identifier format.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: A broad regex can accept unwanted text, while accepting JSON without checking its expected keys can cause later failures.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Use the simplest pattern possible, prefer fullmatch when the whole value must match, and validate required JSON fields before using them.

workedExample.code:
import re

records = [{'title': 'Variables', 'done': True}, {'title': 'Loops', 'done': False}]
completed = [record['title'] for record in records if record['done']]
valid_id = re.fullmatch(r'[A-Z]{2}-\d{3}', 'PY-101') is not None

print(completed)
print(valid_id)
explanation: The comprehension visits each record and keeps a title only when done is true.
The raw string r'...' keeps the regex backslashes readable.
fullmatch requires the entire identifier to follow the pattern: two uppercase letters, a hyphen, and three digits.
is not None converts the match object or None into a clear Boolean.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Test PY-10 and xx-101. Predict why each fails. Then rewrite the comprehension as a normal for loop and compare readability.

procedure: Start with a normal for loop before shortening a transformation into a comprehension.
Use a generator expression when a large stream can be processed one item at a time.
Use raw strings for normal regex patterns.
Prefer fullmatch for whole-value validation, search for finding a pattern anywhere, and match for checks at the beginning.
Treat parsed JSON as untrusted shape until required keys and value types have been checked.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a deeply nested comprehension that nobody can read.
commonMistakes.why: It hides the transformation and makes debugging harder.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use a normal for loop or helper function when there are several decisions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using regex as the only validation for complex business rules.
commonMistakes.why: A pattern can check form but not every meaning or authorization rule.
commonMistakes.avoid: Combine narrow pattern checks with normal program validation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using eval instead of JSON parsing.
commonMistakes.why: eval executes code and is unsafe for external data.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use json.loads or json.load for JSON, then validate the data shape.

lab.title: Filter completed course records
lab.starterCode:
import re

records = [
    {'id': 'PY-101', 'done': True},
    {'id': 'PY-102', 'done': False}
]

# Make a list of ids for completed records.
# Check that every selected id has the expected simple form.
guidedSteps: Write a comprehension that selects completed ids.
Use re.fullmatch with the supplied identifier style.
Explain why a real importer must also validate that id and done keys exist.
checks: The comprehension has a clear value and filter.
The regex uses fullmatch for a whole identifier.
No external data is executed as Python code.
hints: [record['id'] for record in records if record['done']]
A match result is not None when the pattern matched.
lab.solutionExplanation: The comprehension performs one clear selection. The loop keeps validation readable and easy to extend.
challenges: Find the bug: use re.search when the whole identifier must be valid. What extra text could be accepted?
Experiment: change done to True for both records. What does the comprehension return?

projectConnection.milestone: Load structured records, validate their required shape, select usable rows, and report malformed identifiers clearly.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: You can choose a comprehension or a normal loop based on readability and explain why external JSON is validated before use.

assessment.question: When is a normal for loop preferable to a comprehension?
assessment.answer: When the transformation has several steps or becomes hard to read.
assessment.explanation: Readability and maintainability matter more than minimizing lines.

assessment.question: Which regex function checks the whole string?
assessment.explanation: It requires the pattern to cover the entire value.

assessment.question: Why use JSON parsing instead of eval for external data?
assessment.answer: JSON parsing reads data; eval can execute code.
assessment.explanation: External data must not be treated as executable Python.
